independence_rule: Facts were established from the local Book IV chapter text before comparison with production JSON or the Book IV production manifest. Canonical IDs are normalization labels only; reported, intended, mistaken and actual outcomes remain distinct.

facts.description: Jōtarō waits near the Rendaiji approaches, searches the crowd for Otsū and fears Osugi may have harmed her.
Kojirō arrives and predicts that Seijūrō will lose to Musashi based on what he observed at Gojō Bridge.
Akemi and the monkey arrive; Akemi says Kojirō restrained her at Zuzuya and threatened to act as Seijūrō's second against Musashi.
Akemi publicly insists that Musashi is the only man in her heart despite Kojirō's taunts.
A messenger reports Seijūrō's defeat and injury, sending the waiting Yoshioka men toward the field.
Seijūrō is found alive after Musashi's one-stroke victory, with the shoulder catastrophically damaged.
At Seijūrō's request, Kojirō amputates the ruined right arm rather than allow him to be carried home helpless.
After briefly attempting to walk, Seijūrō collapses and is carried away by his followers.
Kojirō continues to control and taunt Akemi while she fears his cruelty but remains in his company.
Musashi leaves Rendaiji dissatisfied with the victory and hopes Seijūrō survives and recovers.
Musashi meets Myōshū gathering greens; she initially senses blood and danger in him.
Musashi joins Kōetsu and Myōshū at an outdoor tea setting.
Kōetsu's tea, bowl and manner expose Musashi to a form of mastery outside swordsmanship.
Musashi realizes his habit of judging human worth primarily through sword skill is an inadequate yardstick.
Kōetsu and Myōshū invite Musashi to stay with the Hon'ami household.

chapters.title: Too Many Kojirōs
physical_locations: road and tree where Matahachi is bound

facts.description: Matahachi drinks near Tōji, envies Musashi's growing fame and again claims the Sasaki Kojirō identity.
Unable to pay for sake and provoked by the dispute, Matahachi cuts off a man's hand.
Gempachi recognizes the pillbox once belonging to Kusanagi Tenki and pursues Matahachi.
Gempachi captures and binds Matahachi, who explains Tenki's death and his taking of Tenki's property and certificate.
Gempachi proposes killing Matahachi so Tenki's family can receive a clear story of vengeance.
The true Kojirō intervenes and prevents Gempachi from killing Matahachi.
Gempachi explains that Tenki had been charged with delivering Kanemaki Jisai's certificate to Kojirō.
Kojirō refuses the inherited certificate, declaring his intention to surpass Jisai and establish his own Ganryū style.
The true Kojirō condemns Matahachi's use of his name and leaves him bound and publicly marked as an impostor.
Denshichirō returns rapidly toward Kyoto after hearing of Seijūrō's defeat.
Denshichirō encounters Matahachi bound to the tree and has him freed.
Matahachi gives Denshichirō a distorted story portraying Musashi as the abductor of his fiancée and himself as a revenge-seeker.
Denshichirō reaches the badly wounded Seijūrō.
The brothers repeatedly invoke their father Yoshioka Kempō, his reputation and the burden of preserving his school.
Seijūrō transfers practical responsibility for the Yoshioka house and its honor to his younger brother.
The Yoshioka side begins preparing Denshichirō's retaliation against Musashi.
Otsū remains effectively confined under Osugi's control at the inn below Kiyomizudera and cannot freely send word or leave.
Akemi unknowingly takes lodging at the same inn; Otsū sees her and recognizes the woman from the Gojō Bridge scene.
A temple messenger delivers Matahachi's letter to Osugi, prompting movement toward Sannen Hill.
Kojirō passes while looking for Akemi and questions Otsū and Osugi about her.
Matahachi confronts Otsū; she rejects reconciliation and explicitly maintains her love for Musashi.
Matahachi draws his sword and pursues Otsū with the intention of killing her.
In darkness Matahachi repeatedly strikes a human figure and he and Osugi believe they have killed Otsū.
The corpse is later identified as an unrelated sick/disturbed rōnin, not Otsū.
Takuan and others search the area; Otsū is found alive but unconscious near the marsh.
Musashi searches unsuccessfully for Rakanji and traces of the Akamatsu ancestry emphasized by his father.
Musashi stays several days with the Hon'ami household and observes sword polishing, books, painting and ceramics.
Kōetsu deepens Musashi's understanding of Liang-k'ai's painting and of artistic mastery.
Kōetsu offers Musashi the Liang-k'ai painting; Musashi declines because a wandering swordsman cannot properly keep it.
The household reports Yoshioka men spying on Musashi and attempting to deliver a threatening letter.
Musashi accompanies Kōetsu and Haiya Shōyū into Yanagimachi and the Ōgiya.
Kōetsu and Shōyū send Karasumaru a linked poem asking that Yoshino join them; Karasumaru replies with blank paper interpreted as snow.
While the others continue drinking and games, Musashi slips away from the parlor for his separate martial obligation.

chapters.title: Reverberations in the Snow
physical_locations: Yanagimachi back exit and Gion route

facts.description: Musashi leaves the Ōgiya by the back, prepares clothing and a fallback note, then moves through Gion toward the appointed site.
Denshichirō and Yoshioka supporters assemble at Rengeōin; he drinks modestly while waiting.
Genzaemon, Kempō's brother and Denshichirō's uncle, arrives and orders the supporters away so the fight will not appear a mass attack.
Hyōsuke refuses to leave completely and hides under the temple floor while Denshichirō waits.
Musashi approaches through the temple, warms himself and takes the veranda position before revealing himself.
Musashi provokes Denshichirō and controls position and tempo before descending into the courtyard.
Musashi and Denshichirō enter a prolonged sword standoff in the snow.
Musashi detects Hyōsuke attacking from behind and kills him first.
In the same rapid sequence Musashi strikes Denshichirō fatally.
As Genzaemon and the Yoshioka followers rush in, Musashi uses the temple buildings and darkness to escape.
Shōyū invades Karasumaru's gathering and turns the dispute over Yoshino into playful class and drinking competition.
Shōyū unexpectedly encounters his old friend Takuan at Karasumaru's parlor.
Takuan reflects that Otsū, rescued after Kiyomizudera, is staying sick at Karasumaru's house while Jōtarō nurses her.
After Musashi returns from the Denshichirō fight, Takuan finds him at the Ōgiya.
Yoshino gathers the disparate guests in her rustic cottage rather than choose between rival patrons.
Yoshino notices and discreetly wipes blood from Musashi's sleeve, recognizing that something dangerous has occurred.

chapters.title: The Broken Lute
historical_context: Po Chü-i lute poem and Heike performance tradition

facts.description: The group writes poems and art as a memento of the peony-fire evening.
Yoshino performs the lute and a passage from the Tales of the Heike.
Yoshino asks Musashi to remain overnight; the request becomes urgent when surveillance reports a large Yoshioka force around the quarter.
A scout reports heavily armed Yoshioka groups at the gate, in nearby streets and around the riding ground, numbering at least roughly one hundred.
Musashi remains awake and rigid through the night while Yoshino tries to persuade him to relax.
Yoshino compares Musashi to a lute whose rigid core would snap rather than resonate, teaching the need for flexibility within strength.
Yoshino deliberately cuts open her lute to show Musashi the flexible crosspiece that gives the instrument tonal richness.
Musashi absorbs Yoshino's warning that excessive rigidity may itself be a fatal martial weakness.
Otsū remains feverish and weak at Karasumaru's house while Jōtarō searches the city for food she can tolerate and nurses her.
A Nansōji monk brings Takuan news that his mother's condition is grave.
Takuan decides to leave immediately for Tajima and asks Karasumaru to continue hosting Otsū and Jōtarō.
Takuan entrusts Otsū to Jōtarō and says her deepest problem is a sickness of the heart rather than merely bodily fever.
Takuan deliberately tells Jōtarō to report that Musashi is infatuated with Yoshino and lingering in the brothel, hoping the truth or shock may change Otsū's fixation.
After quarreling with Takuan, Jōtarō begins searching Kyoto for Yanagimachi and the Ōgiya to find Musashi himself.
Jōtarō reaches the Ōgiya, fights a servant who throws him out and seriously injures him with the wooden sword.
A Yoshino attendant finds Jōtarō and secretly guides him to Musashi's hiding place.
Jōtarō embraces his teacher and tells him how ill Otsū is and how desperately she wants to see him.
Musashi sympathizes but does not promise Jōtarō that he will visit Otsū.
Musashi has his old clothes returned from the Hon'ami household and prepares to leave the shelter.
The attendant explains that the Yoshioka watch is still dense and that Jōtarō's public claim to be Musashi's pupil has reinforced suspicion.
Musashi says he has a plan and arranges for Jōtarō to wait near the rear gate while he says farewell to Yoshino.

chapters.title: The Gate
functional_actors: roughly thirty Yoshioka men at the gate

facts.description: Musashi sends Jōtarō over the wall as a decoy/safe exit while he commits to walking openly through the main gate.
Outside the gate Musashi is surrounded by a large Yoshioka group and challenges them to state whether they seek revenge or a proper bout.
Jūrōzaemon declares that the school intends to kill Musashi to avenge Seijūrō and Denshichirō and restore its name.
Kojirō interrupts the impending street battle and invokes warrior honor and public order to demand a formal time and place.
Musashi accepts any time and place chosen by the Yoshioka side while refusing to place himself in Kojirō's custody.
Musashi rejoins Jōtarō at the Yanagi Riding Grounds after leaving the Yoshioka confrontation.
Musashi travels with Jōtarō to the Karasumaru back gate but refuses to enter even though Otsū is nearby.
Believing he may soon die, Musashi asks Jōtarō to tell Otsū to seek her own happiness and explains that seeing her might break his resolve.
Musashi silently leaves Jōtarō rather than meet Otsū.
Sick Otsū comes outside searching for Jōtarō; he brings her back into the house without revealing the full truth.
Matahachi brings Osugi news of the announced Ichijōji confrontation.
Mother and son plan to reach Ichijōji and obtain a trophy from Musashi's corpse so they can claim fulfillment of their vendetta.
Matahachi unexpectedly discovers Akemi staying at the same inn.
Akemi tells Matahachi that Oko and Gion Tōji ran away together and that she has been living independently.
Akemi flees the inn before paying her bill.
Akemi takes Osugi and Matahachi's travel-money pouch and leaves a note asking Matahachi's pardon for borrowing it.
Despite the loss of money, Osugi and Matahachi depart at night toward Ichijōji.

chapters.title: The Death Trap
physical_locations: three approach roads and surrounding slopes

facts.description: The remaining Yoshioka faction assembles roughly seventy fighters around the spreading pine and three approach roads.
Thirteen-year-old Genjirō is installed under the pine as the formal representative of the Yoshioka house while adults will do the fighting.
The force plans to hide along all three approaches and attack Musashi from multiple directions.
Three archers and one musketeer are positioned to ensure Musashi cannot escape the mass attack.
Kojirō arrives intending to witness the fight, is initially treated as an enemy and nearly clashes with Jūrōzaemon.
Genzaemon apologizes to Kojirō, who pivots to openly encouraging the Yoshioka side.
Kojirō gives the Yoshioka men a hostile profile of Musashi based partly on Akemi's information and advises treating him like a dangerous animal.
Kojirō proposes an additional undisclosed trick to guarantee Musashi actually enters the death trap.
Musashi returns to the cheap inn where he met Jōtarō, prepares fresh underclothes, bathes before dawn and departs for the battle.
A coffin-maker informs Musashi that his uncle Matsuo Kaname has died after a short illness.
Kojirō meets Musashi near the Kamo route and warns him explicitly about the Yoshioka force and mass-battle conditions.
Musashi refuses to recruit seconds, arguing that escalating force would increase public harm without serving swordsmanship.
Musashi deliberately shakes off Kojirō and evaluates alternate approaches rather than taking the obvious Ichijōji road.
After learning of the battle, ill Otsū leaves Karasumaru's house with Jōtarō while retainers search the approaches for Musashi.
Otsū's condition worsens on the mountain road; she collapses and spits blood while still insisting on reaching Musashi.
Jōtarō discovers Musashi reflected in a spring; Musashi brings Otsū water and holds her while she recovers.
Alone with Otsū, Musashi admits that he has long loved and desired her while explaining that his sword and discipline still take precedence.
Otsū says she understands his nature and regards herself as his bride in her heart even if they cannot yet live together.
Musashi leaves for the battle while warning Otsū not to follow him in a despairing death.
Jōtarō's demon-like mask frightens another traveler on the cliff path and produces the scream heard during the farewell.
Matahachi and Osugi become lost in the mountains while trying to reach Ichijōji before dawn.
Hearing the same scream caused by Jōtarō's mask, Matahachi descends into a ravine to investigate.
Matahachi discovers Akemi hiding near a small trout shelter and learns she fled toward Ichijōji after overhearing the battle news.
Akemi apologizes for taking the travel money; Matahachi says he is not angry and does not force her back.
Matahachi recognizes that both he and Akemi have become socially and emotionally unmoored, like stray geese separated from a flock.
Matahachi proposes that he and Akemi abandon their old lives and go east together, preferably to Edo.
Akemi accepts Matahachi's plan and leaves with him rather than continue to Ichijōji.
Matahachi knowingly leaves Osugi behind on the mountain, expecting her eventually to return to Miyamoto after the vendetta.

chapters.title: The Spreading Pine
functional_actors: Ichijōji farmers, woodcutters and priest spectators

facts.description: Kojirō reaches the ambush and warns that Musashi may be using hidden seconds, reinforcing the Yoshioka readiness.
Musashi approaches from above, scouts the spreading pine and identifies the central force and ranged weapons.
At Hachidai Shrine Musashi nearly prays for supernatural protection, stops himself and reframes the episode as a warning against hidden attachment to life.
Musashi attacks from the rear/high ground rather than entering by the expected approach.
Musashi throws a rock that strikes the musketeer's fuse and sends the gunman from the pine before he can fire effectively.
Despite the ambush, Musashi formally announces himself and challenges Genjirō and the Yoshioka force.
Musashi cuts an incoming arrow and immediately closes on the central group.
Musashi deliberately attacks and kills thirteen-year-old Genjirō, the formal standard-bearer of the Yoshioka house.
The Yoshioka force converges; Musashi fights while constantly shifting to exposed corners of their formations.
Under pressure Musashi instinctively draws his short sword and develops the practical basis of a two-sword method against a large force.
Musashi suffers wounds to his knee and forearm but remains combat-effective.
Musashi breaks away through field and woods, deceiving pursuers about his direction and surviving the mass battle.

chapters.title: An Offering for the Dead
historical_context: Oda Nobunaga's destruction of Mount Hiei

facts.description: Musashi recuperates at Mudōji for roughly ten days after arriving wounded and blood-covered.
Haunted especially by Genjirō's death, Musashi carves an image of Kannon as an offering and spiritual exercise.
A group of monks announces that Mount Hiei has reversed its welcome and orders Musashi to leave because of reports about the Ichijōji battle.
The monks condemn Musashi specifically for killing thirteen-year-old Genjirō and argue that true strength should include compassion toward the weak.
Musashi defends the tactical necessity of killing the Yoshioka standard-bearer yet remains profoundly disturbed by the cruelty of the act.
Osugi infiltrates the temple and attacks Musashi at night; he throws the unexpectedly light attacker away before recognizing her.
Musashi recognizes Osugi and infers that she helped turn the monks against him with accusations.
After Osugi is injured in the fall, Musashi carries her inside and nurses her through the night rather than retaliating.
The Mudōji head priest offers a merchant's cow so Musashi can take the ailing Osugi down toward Ōtsu.
Musashi leads the cow carrying Osugi down Mount Hiei, treating her tenderly despite her continuing hatred.
Osugi secretly drinks milk from a local woman, obtains directions and leaves Musashi by a back route.
Musashi sends a letter through the woman asking Otsū to meet him at Kara Bridge in Seta.
At the pass inn Musashi unexpectedly reunites with Matahachi for the first time since Sekigahara.
Musashi challenges Matahachi's habit of blaming others and urges him to make a new start through effort rather than self-pity.
Musashi tells Matahachi to find Osugi and offers to travel east with him afterward so he can rebuild his life.
Matahachi discovers Akemi has left the inn and taken belongings/money rather than remain his companion.
Kojirō lectures stonecutters and Mount Hiei men, systematically minimizing Musashi's Ichijōji achievement and portraying him as unethical and opportunistic.
Musashi reveals he overheard Kojirō's critique; their polite exchange functions as an unmistakable promise of a future clash.

chapters.title: Entwining Branches
historical_context: Taiheiki story of Shiga priest used in Musashi's reflection

facts.description: Otsū says that after the moonlight meeting she no longer needs to chase Musashi; she trusts their bond even while separated.
A Karasumaru retainer delivers Musashi's first direct letter asking Otsū to meet him in Seta.
Otsū and Jōtarō immediately leave the hermitage and travel via Shiga Pass toward Lake Biwa and Seta.
Musashi enters Ōtsu, arranges to rent the cow onward and travels toward Seta expecting Otsū.
The three reunite at Kara Bridge, where Otsū and Jōtarō have arrived first.
Musashi imagines traveling to Edo with Otsū and Jōtarō, with Otsū receiving education while he continues martial discipline.
While Matahachi tries to meet Musashi at Seta, Kojirō has him brought into a brothel and attempts to dissuade him from siding with Musashi against Osugi.
Kojirō and the women keep Matahachi drinking until he passes out, causing him to miss the planned Seta reunion.
Matahachi reaches Seta too late and finds Musashi's note saying to catch up on the road east.
Matahachi follows the Nakasendō through Kusatsu, Hikone, Toriimoto and Suribachi Pass, repeatedly searching side roads for Musashi.
Near Nakatsugawa Matahachi finally sees Musashi but discovers Otsū riding with him; jealousy reverses his renewed friendship into resentment.
The three travel near Magome Pass and stop beside the Male and Female Waterfalls.
Musashi asks whether Otsū might still choose Matahachi; she emphatically rejects the possibility.
Overcome by desire, Musashi grabs Otsū and throws her backward onto the grass.
Otsū resists in alarm and flees the immediate scene; Musashi is shocked and ashamed by his loss of self-control.
Musashi recognizes sexual desire as an internal adversary that his sword cannot defeat.
Musashi strips and stands under the heavy waterfall in a severe purification/discipline exercise.
Otsū and Jōtarō separately witness Musashi under the falls and fear for his life.
Musashi emerges spiritually steadier, using the ordeal to recommit himself to discipline.
Otsū gathers Musashi's clothes and swords in the hut while Jōtarō waits nearby, sensing the gravity of what has occurred.
